questions.question: When you switch a ZK application from Groth16 to a Plonk-family SNARK, what should ideally remain unchanged?
options: The proof system backend implementation
The relation/circuit (what is being proven)
The verifier's public-input ordering
The field/curve arithmetic used by the circuit
questions.explanation: A good architecture keeps the relation stable and swaps only the proving backend and its parameters.

questions.question: In the common R1CS witness vector layout z = [1, public..., witness...], what is z[0]?
options: A random blinding value
A constant wire fixed to 1
The first public input
The circuit output value
questions.explanation: z[0] is the constant 1 wire used to encode constants inside linear combinations.

questions.question: Which R1CS constraint shape encodes an addition gate c = a + b in this lesson's toy compiler?
options: a * b = c
questions.explanation: Addition is a linear relation; using the constant-1 wire turns it into the R1CS form A*B=C.

questions.question: What does it mean if `first_unsatisfied(constraints, z, p)` returns `None`?
options: The witness vector is missing some variables
All constraints are satisfied by z (mod p)
The circuit has no public inputs
The constraint system is underdetermined
questions.explanation: Returning None means every constraint evaluated to zero, so the R1CS is satisfied.

questions.question: Why is 'public input ordering drift' a real bug in ZK systems?
options: It changes the cryptographic security level of the curve
It makes the prover slower but still correct
It binds the proof to a different statement than the verifier thinks
It only affects human-readable logs, not verification
questions.explanation: Verifiers interpret public inputs as an ordered vector; reordering changes the statement being verified.

questions.question: What is the main risk if a circuit constant becomes an unconstrained witness variable?
options: The verifier can no longer deserialize the proof
The prover can choose the 'constant' value to make false statements pass
The circuit becomes constant-time and safer
The constraint count necessarily decreases
questions.explanation: An unconstrained 'constant' is effectively free choice, which can let the prover satisfy constraints for unintended statements.

questions.question: You have both native witness generation code and an R1CS gadget for the same operation. What is the failure mode if they implement different specs?
options: Everything still works because SNARKs are probabilistic
The prover may compute a witness that doesn't satisfy the constraints, so proving fails
The verifier becomes unable to check public inputs
The field modulus automatically adjusts to match
questions.explanation: If native computation and constraints drift, you can generate values that look right but do not satisfy the constraint system.

questions.question: Attack scenario: the circuit intends to enforce out = x^3 + x + 5, but the value '5' is allocated as a witness and never constrained. What can a malicious prover do?
options: Nothing; the backend will treat it as a constant anyway
Choose the '5' witness to make any (x, out) pair satisfy the circuit
Force the verifier to accept without checking constraints
Recover the verifier's secret key from the proof
questions.explanation: If the constant is free, the prover can set it to whatever makes the equality hold, changing the statement being proven.
